title: Playing records for Jelly, and interviewing Willie the Lion Smith
summary: In one long block Russell recounts Hullsizer quizzing Jelly about records, Jelly preferring to play his new songs, and later paying Willie the Lion for an interview.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: By the time I met him, I had probably three-fourths of his records. I remember when, just by way of introduction, I was just about as bad as Hullsizer, who used to play all the Jelly records for Jelly. You'd take him over to his house, Jelly, over to Hullsizer's house. Hullsizer was a record collector from Ohio and happened to be living in Washington about the 1938 period, too. And he'd play all of these records and ask Jelly who's on this record and, you know, tried to get personnel. Jelly couldn't remember some of them. He was confused. They'd been made, oh, 10 to 12 years before most of them. So Jelly wasn't really too interested, either. And so after an hour or so of that, he could tell Jelly was really fed up and he'd go over and look out of the window down at his car. So then Hullsizer said he knew it was time to quit. So I also began talking about records to Jelly and told him that I had a lot of the records and mentioned some of the titles. And I remember he seemed interested at that time that I had those. He went in back to the kitchen, a woman by the name of Mrs. Lyle had started this place called the Jungle Inn, it was called the Music Box when I went there in 1938. And he said, oh, here's the man that's got all of my records. He went back. Actually, he'd had a few of his records on the Jukebox even at that time. I think they were Hullsizers, I didn't know it at the time, but some of the Bluebird reissues mostly. And I remember even he played some of them one night when Charles Smith and I were there. So in a way he liked his records, but yet they didn't impress him that much. I mean, to him it was just another job and he was more interested in promoting his new music. He played for me the first time I wanted to hear all the old classics, you might say, the King Porter and Wolverine and the Pearls, and he played all those for me. But as soon as he'd finished one of those, then he'd start playing some of these new pieces. I remember on the piano he had the manuscript of Sweet Substitute, which he had supposedly just written, I guess. I didn't know Roy Carew in those days at all. Who he was, I'd never met him. I didn't know he was going to publish those things even. But Jelly was much more interested in those new songs and things that he was working on. Of course he had the idea that they might go over in jukeboxes and all. And naturally, I mean, if everybody else was making money with the jukebox records, he thought he deserved a chance too. And the Sweet Substitute and some of those other tunes are wonderful tunes too, actually. Sweet Substitute in particular. Yet I wasn't interested in hearing those. I wanted to hear the old ones that night. But I'm just trying to show his attitude usually to records as just something that's gone in the past. It reminds me of Willie the Lion when I wanted to interview him. This book on Jelly Roll that I've been working on now for about six years, I haven't been working much on the last few years, really. But I interviewed Willie about 1970. And I had an awful time getting him. The New York phone system is so bad then you couldn't get half of the numbers, it seems like. I'd been calling Willie for about, oh, roughly three or four days. Every day I'd call him two or three times. Could never get an answer. Always a busy signal or something, just a funny buzz. So finally I called him from a phone up in Harlem and I got him right away. So I told him I wanted to interview him about Jelly. And I paid for all these interviews, usually at the rate of $25 an interview. And I didn't get time to tell him I was going to pay him anything yet. He thought it was going to be another guy, a record collector, somebody bothering him, you know. So he started in with a good lecture to me. We can't be bothered. We of the living, you know. We have our lives to live. Those things, those days are gone. It's all gone. He's not going to talk about Jelly. So finally I told him that Don Ewell, he'd just made a long play record with Don up in Toronto. And they worked at a club together. A lot of two piano work they did. So I mentioned Don Ewell in a hurry that he'd given me his address. In fact, he had two addresses. One was his lady friend. And then I told him right away that I would pay him. And I said I'd been paying $25, but I knew that he was more important than most. You know, he's got this idea, had this idea of his importance, which he was important, of course, too, and a good pianist. One of the best in Holland. So I said I'd be glad to pay him $50 for the interview, which was twice the usual amount. Because I knew that he ordinarily didn't want to talk. He didn't. One day, I mean one year, he wouldn't come down here to the jazz festival because they didn't pay him enough. He'd first agreed to come, sort of a verbal agreement that he would come down. Then he got thinking about later that he should have a few hundred dollars more or something for it. So he didn't show up. So I knew those things, so that's why I offered him the $50. But as soon as I mentioned $50, he didn't say yes or anything. He said, it's got to be in cash. It's got to be in cash. So I said, yeah, I got it with me. And so he told me to come right on over. He was very nice. He talked for an hour. He wasn't that commercial a guy. I'm not trying to imply that all he thought about was money.
